To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the energy-GDP nexus for OECD countries is not cointegrated and that there is Granger noncausality from GDP to energy and from energy to GDP.
there is no evidence of long-term cointegration between energy and GDP, and that there is little or no evidence of short-term Granger-causality running in either direction between them.
the data are not cointegrating and there is no Granger-causality between energy use and GDP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the question of whether the relationship between energy and GDP is a long-run equilibrium relationship, and if so, what is the nature of causality between the two variables.
the question of whether there is a long-term relationship between energy use and economic growth, and if so, which direction the causality runs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
energy-GDP causality is not a robust finding in the OECD.
the relation of energy to GDP in developed economies is weak, but not insignificant.

there is no evidence of energy-GDP causality for the developed economies examined here, and thus, there is no reason to believe that the energy-GDP relationship in the developing economies would be different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
energy and GDP are not as tightly linked as often assumed, and that energy and per capita GDP are also not as tightly linked, especially for road and residential sectors.
energy and GDP are not as closely linked as is commonly believed.
there is no evidence of energy-GDP causality in either direction, and there is little evidence of energy-GNP cointegration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to reconsider the energy-GDP nexus, especially for developed countries.
there is a need to rethink the energy-GDP relationship in a way that is more nuanced and flexible than is currently the case.
there is no reason for the energy-GDP relation to be linear or to be a simple function of GDP per capita.
